3804.dq: (1) No Heiltsuk word, lexical or combined with clitics, features more than 3 high tones [p.314]; ... The first /V/ of the phonemic word bears accent [p.315, Oowekyala]
3804.dloc: Rath 1985 p.313 (opening paragraph), p.314 (rules 1-5), pp.315-316 (Oowekyala accent rule and its exception clause), p.317 (rule 6b), p.318 (rule 3b exemptions; proclitics low; lexical-high-tone residue). Also read: Rath 1974 (pp.47-49); Wilson 1987 (pp.321-324).
3804.prule: Heiltsuk proper (Bella Bella/Waglisla, Klemtu): two phonemic tones, high vs low, with tonal minimal pairs, distinctive only on unglottalized vowels (glottalized vowels V̓ always low); high-tone placement is largely rule-governed within the phonemic word (lexical word plus clitics): at most 3 high tones per word (rule 1; when there are three the last two sit in a tripleton VRV, rule 2); a doubleton VV always takes a high tone unless rules 1/2/5 forbid (3b, with listed exemptions); no high tone after a doubleton/VaV/tripleton (5); the first V that is a singleton both phonemically and morphophonemically takes high tone and later ones low (6b); a first singleton deriving morphophonemically from a glottalized vowel */V̓/ is low (6a, except suffix-final before #/T/R-enclitic); proclitics always low; a residue of lexical high tone in certain suffix/enclitic allomorphs. No separate stress rule: Rath 1974 sec. 3.3 states that length and accent (stress) are 'linked with pitch and predictable'.
3804.srule: Not mentioned in Rath 1985 (ICSNL 20, pp.313-323, read in full) or Rath 1974 secs 3.2-3.3 (pp.47-49): the sources describe tone (high/low) with accent 'linked with pitch and predictable' and say nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress; Wilson 1986 (BLS 12) p.287: 'the status of secondary stress is unclear'.

3804.tone: Rath 1985 p.313: Heiltsuk phonemes 'include a high tone and a low tone', minimal pairs /k'as/ 'mussels' vs /k'as/ 'sit outside', /yimas/ 'chief' vs its plural; 'most instances of the Heiltsuk tones have turned out to be predictable in terms of phonotactic and morphophonemic parameters'. Rath 1974 sec. 3.2 (p.47): 'Prosodic features noted were pitch, length, and accent (stress)'; 3.2.2 (p.49): 'Accent can be heard in words with a pitch-contour... The place of the accent, however, appears to be a matter of dialect' (Mr. Freeman keeps 'the accent with the first high-pitched vowel', Mr. Campbell differs); 3.3: 'both length and accent are linked with pitch and predictable... Pitch, for that matter, is no doubt phonemic' (scan renders 'accent' as 'and~.nt' in 3.3). Wilson 1987 pp.323-324: 'Heiltsuq has two tones, high and low... A maximum of three high-toned syllables can occur in a word'; 'tone assignment is not predictable from synchronic segmental information, and a number of minimal pairs distinguished only by tone exist'; H tone corresponds to the common-Wakashan primary-stress position (first heavy syllable) and never falls to its right. Rath 1985 p.320 (per the compilers; not re-read here) reserves 'pitch accent' for Haisla (hais1244). System is left-edge-computed and bounded (max 3 H) but not culminative; all sources call it tone.

3805.dq: Vandermeiren p. 11: 'nous donnerons à chaque mot, autant que faire se peut, son accent tonique' (dictionary citation forms; 'certains mots, en tout semblables pour l'orthographe, ont des sens totalement différents d'après la place qu'on donne à l'accent tonique'). 3805.dloc: Vandermeiren 1913, Introduction §V, p. 11 (Gallica ark:/12148/bd6t5358164w, canvas f19, page scan). Colle 1913, tome II, E, a, 124 'Langage', p. 661, continued on p. 662 (Internet Archive lesbalubacongobe02coll).
3805.prule: No stress rule is stated. The word 'accent tonique' is lexically placed and contrastive: words identical in spelling differ in meaning by the place of the accent (Vandermeiren), and Colle states outright that this word accent 'n'est pas l'accent prosodique' but a musical high pitch ('le do aigu') that falls on the penult or the antepenult depending on the word (lùbuzi, bàluba vs kamùntu), 'likewise for shorter and longer words'. Read together the sources describe a Bantu tone / pitch-accent system with a lexically distributed high pitch and no dynamic word stress.
3805.srule: Deciding 1913 sources: not mentioned (Vandermeiren 1913 p. 11 silent; Colle 1913 II p. 661: a trisyllable has 'deux sons graves et un son aigu', i.e. one high per word). Vandermeiren 1912 §54: words with a quadrisyllabic radical carry, besides the main accent on the first radical syllable, 'un second accent sur la pénultième' (kusótolóla, kuvúngulúla, kusíntakánya); if the verb derives from a simple verb accented on the prefix ku-, the main accent stays on ku- and the second accent falls on the antepenult (kúfumúnuna, kúkutúlula). Otherwise one accent per word (§41), except reduplicated radicals, which repeat it on each copy (§47 lémbalémba, kambalámbalá). Same pitch 'accent' as the primary (coded tonal), not a dynamic secondary stress.

3805.tone: Colle 1913 II: 661-662: every word carries an accent 'qui n'est pas l'accent prosodique, mais l'accent tonique, musical, ou aigu', i.e. the raised note ('le do aigu'); a trisyllable has two low ('graves') and one high ('aigu') syllable, the high falling on the penult or the antepenult depending on the word; the drum/whistle language is built on this high pitch plus long/semi-long/short syllable length ('non seulement de l'accent tonique et musical, mais encore de la longueur des syllabes'). Vandermeiren 1913 calls the same thing 'accent tonique' and marks it in the dictionary together with vowel length (acute = short, grave = long). Blakely 1981 (ERIC ED250944, p. 2 footnote, saved) writes Kihemba with high, lowered-high, low, rising and falling tone marks. Neither 1913 source uses the word 'ton'; the 'stress' of the reading is Colle's negative statement that the accent is not prosodic (dynamic).

tn.quote: Chaque mot comporte un accent, qui n'est pas l'accent prosodique, mais l'accent tonique, musical, ou aigu. Ces trois derniers mots désignent cette même inflexion élevée (le do aigu). Voici un mot de trois syllabes; il possède deux sons graves et un son aigu; le son aigu frappe soit la pénultième, soit l'antipénultième; on dira, par exemple: lùbuzi (une grande chèvre), bàluba, avec l'accent aigu sur lù et sur bà; ou bien kamùntu (un petit homme), avec l'accent aigu sur mù. Il en est de même des mots plus courts et plus longs.
tn.translation: Every word carries an accent, which is not the prosodic (stress) accent but the tonic, musical, or acute accent. These last three words designate the same raised inflection (the high 'do'). Here is a word of three syllables; it has two low sounds and one high sound; the high sound strikes either the penultimate or the antepenultimate; one says, for example: lùbuzi (a big goat), bàluba, with the acute accent on lù and on bà; or kamùntu (a small man), with the acute accent on mù. The same holds for shorter and longer words.
tn.cite: Colle, R. P. [Pierre] (1913). Les Baluba (Congo belge), tome II. Collection de Monographies ethnographiques XI (publiée par Cyr. van Overbergh). Bruxelles: Albert Dewit / Institut International de Bibliographie.

tn.note: Each word carries one musical accent: a high pitch ('le do aigu') on one syllable, the rest low; its place (penult, antepenult or prefix) is lexical and distinguishes words; no dynamic stress apart.

3807.prule: No word-stress position rule. Hezhou/Linxia is a three-tone language: citation tones ping = low rising (23 for the 2010 Linxia-city informant), shang = high level (44), qu = high falling (42), with the shang/qu values swapped at some localities. Disyllabic items (二字句) fall into two sandhi types: A-type, where both syllables are read with about equal strength and keep their citation tone values fairly well, and B-type, where either the first or the second syllable sounds stressed and the unstressed syllable's tone value is heavily deformed or its tone class neutralised. Stress judgements are given for three patterns only and only as auditory impressions: 23-21 (§2.1.2 '聴覚印象的には、第一音節に強勢がある'; §2.2.2 'やはり第一音節に強勢が感じられる') and 44-21 (§2.3.3 '第一音節に強勢が感じられる') have first-syllable stress, 21-34 (§2.1.3 '聴覚印象的には、第二音節に強勢がある') has second-syllable stress. 44-42 carries no stress judgement anywhere (§2.3.2 describes its distribution only); it is A-type in the Ⅱ/Ⅲ + Ⅱ/Ⅲ combinations (p.48 '[Ⅱ+Ⅲ]は 44-42 のみで、[Ⅲ+Ⅲ]は 44-42(A 型)') and B-type only in Ⅱ+Ⅰ (B-type table, p.48). Which type and pattern a given word takes is not predictable from its tone classes (帮忙 23-23, 聪明 21-34, 工人 23-21 are all qing-ping + zhuo-ping); the author states only that verb-object phrases are almost all A-type (p.48) and that 21-34 occurs mainly when the second syllable is a historical zhuo-ping. Stress is reported as an auditory impression tied to the sandhi type, not as an independent positional rule.

The source analyses only monosyllables and disyllables and speaks of a strong vs weak syllable within B-type disyllables (first syllable strong in 23-21 and 44-21, second in 21-34), never of secondary or rhythmic stress.

3807.tone: Three lexical tones (ping/shang/qu; MC ru mostly merged into ping, a few into qu). Sarashina's tabulation of earlier descriptions (p.43): Ma Shujun 1982 平13 上44 去53; Li 1984 24/44/42; Lanzhou 1996 243/43/42; Chen 1999 Jishishan 34/44/42, Xunhua 23/42/44; Dang et al. 2006 Linxia city 132/554/43, Yongjing two-tone 13/53. Citation tones of the young informant are unstable, 44 vs 42 often merge, and an utterance-final fall independent of tone obscures them; Chen 1999:254 is quoted (carried) as saying that in single syllables read alone the tonal features 'become very blurred, even disappear entirely' (声调特征变得十分模糊，甚至完全消失). Disyllabic sandhi is complex (patterns 23-23, 23-21, 21-34, 23-42, 21-42, 44-23, 44-42, 44-21); B-type neutralises the second syllable's tone like Mandarin neutral tone but, unlike Mandarin, also has a weak-strong type (21-34). Author links the small, unstable tone inventory to the toneless Mongolic, Turkic and Tibetan neighbours. Zhang 2009 (Linxia city, Han and Hui accents): 声调 3 个: 平声 13 上声 33 去声 51; reduplicated nouns have neutral tone on the second syllable (名词重叠，后一个音节读轻声, e.g. 巷巷 hã51 hã0). Kawasumi 2018 fn.42 quotes Lee-Smith 1996:865 ('in the process of acquiring tones') and rejects it.

3808.tone: No tone system. The sources speak of an 'accent'; Melchert 1993 (JIES 21: 254) says the Anatolian accent 'contains an element of stress as well as pitch', and the Luvian lengthening rule shows the stress component. The acute/grave marks in hieroglyphic transliteration (sa, sá, sà) are homophone indices, not prosody (Payne 2010: 13; Kammenhuber 1969: 152 n. 1; Werner 1991: 16).

3809.prule: Word stress is phonemic (contrastive): minimal pairs differ by stress placement alone ('sa.la 'punishment' vs sa.'la 'sin'; 'su.led 'sibling' vs su.'led 'inside'). Its own segmental tables nonetheless carry two trisyllables with initial (antepenultimate) stress, so even the stated two-syllable window is not data-consistent.

3810.dq: Clitics occur at the outer edges of the words to which they attach and are extra-metrical. That is, they do not take stress. ... In (2.135a) the stress falls on the ante-penultimate syllable of the stressable word, which consists of the verb root ... 'bathe' and the inflectional suffix -pa; the clitic +nam occurs at the edge of the stressable word. [pp. 91, 93]
3810.heavy: Primary stress: a final syllable of shape CVVC[+nasal], i.e. long vowel plus consonant coda ('A number of morphemes that affix to roots are of the shape CVVC[+nasal], which are heavy and attract stress', p. 94), and a final syllable closed by the completive /-W/ ('it would make the syllable heavy', p. 96). Plain CVC or open finals do not attract primary stress (['suk.suk] 'river', ['kuʔj.puk] 'achiote', [puk'tuː.ku] 'clothes'). Tertiary stress uses a broader definition: 'the heaviest syllable (i.e. containing a long vowel or a closed syllable)' (p. 88).
3810.dflt: penultimate syllable of the stressable word (clitics excluded); monosyllabic roots stressed on the root
3810.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stressable word (stem plus affixes; proclitics and enclitics are extrametrical), except that a heavy final syllable of shape CVVC[+nasal] (long vowel plus coda, e.g. =hoːm 'in', -tɛːn 'two') takes primary stress; the completive suffix /-W/ (posited underlying /-wɨ/, surface [wɨ]~[u]~[o]~zero) is analysed as making the final syllable heavy and so stressed ([tɔ.ˈgɔj] 'it is lost', [nɨm.ˈjah] 'they said'); Spanish loans keep source stress (kapéel 'coffee', ʔabríl 'April', galán); vocatives take final stress ([pɨ.ˈʃiːɲ] 'Man!'). Monosyllabic roots carry the stress ([ʔaʔ.ˈnaj] 'my leaf').
3810.srule: Secondary stress on the leftmost syllable of the stressable word, i.e. the first syllable after any proclitics (clitics are never stressed); not assigned in a trisyllabic word with penultimate primary (2.134c). A tertiary stress falls on the heaviest syllable (long vowel or closed) between secondary and primary stress, leftmost if of equal weight; the author hedges this ('some exceptions but no definitive experiments have been done') and notes that word-medial clitics in compounds (2.147) do not follow the weight prediction.

3813.dloc: White 2021: §2.11 Summary, p. 76 (domain statement); the prominence is placed 'on the final syllable of a phonological word' at §2.8 Pragmatic prominences, p. 70, and §3.1.1 Word-level pragmatic prominence, pp. 80-81. page numbers are the running heads at the top of each page.
3813.prule: No lexical stress. White Hmong is a seven-tone language with a strong bias to monosyllabic words (§2.3, §3.1); the author states that if every monosyllabic word had lexical stress 'there will be no meaningful contrast in lexical stress' (§3.1 p. 79) and posits none. The only word-level prominence is an optional, pragmatically conditioned prominence (new or important information) that 'tends to be placed on the final syllable of a phonological word' (iambic-like): the prominent vowel resists reduction, is longer and may carry an expanded pitch range for its tone (§2.8 p. 70: deb deb 'be very far', txom nyem 'be impoverished'; §3.1.1 tua tua 'shoot repeatedly'); it disappears in careful slow speech and in rapid speech (p. 80) and serves as a wordhood diagnostic. Whitelock 1982 p. 37 (reduplicated verbs/adjectives: second copy stressed, longer, higher; first copy reduced) agrees.
3813.srule: No secondary stress rule is stated. Four-syllable elaborate expressions with two prominences (second and fourth syllables) 'are best analysed as two phonological words', confirmed by pause placement (§3.1.1 p. 85, §3.1.2); §2.9's intensification process (expanded pitch range, lengthening) is a separate process, not a secondary stress. Exception to the final-syllable prominence: the clause-final enclitic =os ‘CFM:SOFT’ lacks prominence, which appears on the syllable before it (§3.1.3 p. 88).

The contour of the tone is also changed - the first word having a shorter contour and the second word usually long and drawn out and on a higher pitch than the basic tone.'

3815.dq: No stress statement exists, so no stress domain is stated. The tonal data are word-level (verb radicals, noun stems and short verb forms cited in isolation): 'On peut observer, dans les formes suivantes, que les tons structurels des radicaux verbaux du holoholo sont identiques à ceux attestés en protobantou, à cela près qu'ils se déplacent vers la droite d'une syllabe'.
3815.dloc: §2 'TONALITE', p. 324 (extracted-article p. 8; volume p. 320), continuing to p. 326, page 8 read as an image
3815.prule: Tone language: two level tones (H 'haut', B 'bas') plus a rising tone (A 'ascendant') arising from tone shift. Proto-Bantu stem tones are preserved but realised one or two syllables to the right of their etymological position (verb radicals: shift of one syllable; noun stems: *HH > BH, *HB > BH, *BH > BA or BB; the vacated syllable takes a low morphotoneme; all-low stems unchanged). No stress or accent rule is stated anywhere in the article; the words accent, intensité, pénultième, proéminence do not occur.
3815.quote: 2. TONALITE. Sur le plan tonal, le holoholo a conservé en général les tons du protobantou. On peut observer, dans les formes suivantes, que les tons structurels des radicaux verbaux du holoholo sont identiques à ceux attestés en protobantou, à cela près qu'ils se déplacent vers la droite d'une syllabe: [...] Le holoholo atteste en effet un déplacement tonal généralisé des tons vers la droite d'une ou de deux syllabes. Voici quelques exemples: ku-tw'al-à kutwalâ porter [...] Ce phénomène semble avoir fonctionné sur le plan historique dans les thèmes nominaux; les tons se sont en effet déplacés…
3815.loc: §2 'TONALITE', p. 324 (extracted-article p. 8; volume p. 320), continuing to p. 326, page 8 read as an image
3815.idn: holoholo, 'parlée dans la région de Kalemie au Shaba' (DR Congo); data: Second-hand: all synchronic data from Coupez, A. 1955, Esquisse de la langue holoholo (Tervuren); the author states he could not consult any Holoholo informant ('nous n’en avons rencontré aucun dans notre entourage immédiat', p. 317). Place/date…
3815.exq_: No stress rule, hence no stress exceptions. Tonal only: 'Pour les autres thèmes à ton(s) bas (type °B ou °BB), les tons sont ceux du protobantou' (p. 326), i.e. all-low stems do not undergo the shift; the author adds 'Ce point mérite une étude approfondie' about the apparent tone inversion.
3815.tone: The source treats Holoholo purely as a H/L tone language with a rising tone from H-shift and a generalized rightward tone shift of one or two syllables (pp. 324-326), possibly 'la clé de l'inversion tonale attestée en zone L'. It says nothing about stress, accent, intensity or a penultimate prominence (a full-text search of the whole article text: no hits for accent/intensit/pénult/stress/proémin). The only other prosodic material is vowel quantity (morphophonème de quantité, compensatory lengthening, pp. 321-323), which is segmental/historical, not stress-related.

3817.dq: Lediglich bei Mehrsilblern und in der Klise läßt sich ein Druckakzent nachweisen, der auf der ersten geschlossenen Silbe des Intervalls sitzt. ... Auch im Satz bleibt der Wortakzent bestehen. Ein weiterer Akzent liegt dann auf der nächsten schweren Silbe. ... Ein Satzakzent läßt sich nicht belegen.
3817.dloc: Teil II Das Hone, Lautlehre, ch. 2 Phonologie und Morphophonologie, §2.5 'Der Akzent', p. 80 (DNB table-of-contents, line '2.5 Der Akzent 80'; running header '80 5 Der Akzent' in the excerpt), examples (189)-(193); tone in §2.4 'Der Ton', pp. 73-79 (ex. 174, Tabelle 10) and §4.1 Zusammenfassung. Text seen only as Google Books-view excerpts (volume C6QaAQAAIAAJ, Atom feed dc:description; dc:creator Anne Storch, dc:date 1999), stitched in document order from overlapping excerpts.
3817.heavy: 'geschlossene Silbe' (closed syllable, CVC): 'Bei Lexemen der Struktur CVCVC gilt dabei die zweite Silbe als geschlossen (CV-CVC) und somit als Akzentträger'; 'Lexeme der Struktur CVCCVC, die somit aus mehreren geschlossenen bzw. schweren Silben bestehen' (closed = heavy); and 'schwere Silbe mit einem langen Vokal oder Diphthong' (CVV), which takes the stress only 'Folgen mehrere offene Silben in der Klise aufeinander'. §2.4 Tabelle 10 equates heavy with bimoraic ('zweimorige (schwere) Silben', 'einmorige (leichte) Silben').
3817.dflt: Initial. All-light disyllables stress the first syllable: 'Zweisilbige Lexeme der Struktur CVCV tragen einen Druckakzent auf der ersten Silbe, die auch in der Klise Akzentträger bleibt' (ex. 190 wūrà 'Frau', bìrì 'Termite'); VCV lexemes likewise stress the first syllable (the prefix vowel), the accent shifting in clisis to the next, 'scheinbar schwere' syllable (ex. 191 àsà 'Blut', abū 'Ding', àyé 'Säugling'). Monosyllables (most roots and lexemes) show 'kaum Akzentrealisierungen' (hardly any stress realisation) outside discourse.
3817.prule: In polysyllabic words and clitic groups (the 'Intervall') a non-contrastive dynamic stress (Druckakzent) falls on the first closed syllable of the domain: in CVCVC lexemes the second syllable counts as closed (CV-CVC) and is therefore the stress-bearer; lexemes of the shape CVCCVC, consisting of several closed i.e. heavy syllables, take the stress on the first syllable. If several open syllables follow one another in the clitic group, stress falls on the first heavy syllable with a long vowel or diphthong. All-light disyllables take the stress on the first syllable: CVCV lexemes stress the first syllable, which remains the stress-bearer in clisis too (ex. 190 wūrà 'Frau', bìrì 'Termite'); VCV lexemes stress the first syllable, i.e. the prefix vowel (in isolation often giving the false impression of a high-toned prefix vowel), and in clisis the accent shifts to the next, 'apparently heavy' syllable (ex. 191 àsà ní, àyémíí). Monosyllables, which make up most roots and lexemes, show hardly any stress realisation outside discourse.
3817.srule: Not described within the word in Storch 1999, §2.5 'Der Akzent', pp. 80-82 (one Druckakzent per polysyllable or clitic group; no 'Nebenakzent'/'Sekundärakzent' anywhere in the volume). Only at sentence level: 'Auch im Satz bleibt der Wortakzent bestehen. Ein weiterer Akzent liegt dann auf der nächsten schweren Silbe.' (the word stress persists in the sentence; a further accent then lies on the next heavy syllable).

Zweisilbige Lexeme der Struktur CVCV(V) und CVCVC sind hier besonders häufig. Dabei wird der Druckakzent fast immer auf der zweiten, schweren Silbe hörbar. Bei Lehnwört…
3817.tone: Hone is a tone language; tone, not stress, is the primary word prosody. §2.4 'Der Ton' (pp. 73-79): 'Der Ton hat sowohl lexikalische als auch grammatikalische Funktionen.'; 'Der Ton ist Bestandteil der Silbe und kann von einem Vokal oder einem Nasal getragen werden. Die kleinste tontragende Einheit ist... jedoch die More, so daß schwere Silben grundsätzlich mehr als einen Ton tragen, wobei diese Töne identisch sein können; vgl.: Tabelle 10: Tondistribution in ein- und zweimorigen Silben' (mora = TBU, heavy = bimoraic). tn.translation: 2.4 TONE. Hone is a register-tone language with three tone levels. Tonemically distinctive are a high tone [mark], a mid tone [mark] and a low tone [mark]. Dynamic tones (contour tones) also occur, but are always to be understood as a sequence of two different register tones. Tone has both lexical and grammatical functions. ... Tone is a constituent of the syllable and can be carried by a vowel or a nasal. The smallest tone-bearing unit, however, is ... the mora, so that heavy syllables in principle carry more than one tone

3820.heavy: Not applicable: '(f) Non-moraic: independent of syllable weight.' (p. 316); the conditioning property is tone ([H] > first syllable > other syllables in the prominence hierarchy (257c)).
3820.dflt: Analogue for tone: 'If there are no [H] tones, then stress the leftmost syllable' (rule 261b), i.e. initial (stem-initial per fn 168) stress in words without [H].
3820.prule: Tone-conditioned word stress (metrical, prominence-based analysis after Hayes 1995): primary stress falls on the leftmost [H]-toned syllable of the phonological word (End Rule Left); if the word has no [H] tone, stress falls on the leftmost syllable (of the stem). Stress is obligatory, culminative (one primary per phonological word), predictable, autonomous, demarcative from the left edge, non-moraic (quantity-insensitive) and audible (elevated pitch and intensity; stressed syllables never undergo high-vowel deletion). Because [H] attracts stress, main stress 'does not fall at a fixed distance from the edges' (unbounded). Not computable from syllable count or weight; the conditioning factor is lexical/grammatical tone.
3820.srule: Every [H]-toned syllable is stressed; in a word with more than one [H], the leftmost [H] takes main stress and the remaining [H]-toned syllables carry secondary stress ('secondary-stressed [H] tones'); placement by tone, not rhythm or weight; words without multiple [H] tones have a single stress (no secondary stress in words lacking [H]).

3827.tone: Lexical tone language. Syllable-level tones H, L, <HL> (falling); rising <LH> absent (tone-flattening *…L.H > …L, with a floating +H preserved in some morphological contexts); stem/word melodies {H}, {L}, {HL}, {LHL}; {LH}/{LLH} disallowed 'in any form' (p. 51); extensive tone sandhi (left-to-right and right-to-left spreading, Final-L Delinking, downstep, presuffixal Cv: tone-raising). Ch. 3 Phonology (§3.1–3.10) has no stress, accent, metrical or prosody section; §3.9 Tonology (pp. 51–110) is the only suprasegmental section. 'Stress' occurs phonologically only at (a) p. 258: phonetic first-syllable stress on prosodically heavy gà:-y-ndì, gà:-n-dòŋ 'that can sound like H-tones', which Heath analyses as L-toned; (b) p. 100: kûl 'all' is 'nearly always rhetorically "stressed"', with the preceding word's pitch lowered to frame it — Heath's tone-process summary table calls this leftward downstep 'a device to make the emphatic word "y" more prominent, and is essentially intonational rather than tonal', and before ex. (64) he writes 'I regard this as rhetorical (intonational) and phonetically variable rather than categorically phonological (tonal) in nature'; (c) non-phonological uses ('stressed forms of the imperfective (positive) morpheme', 'the understressed, low-pitched, nontemporal ‘now’', 'glossed in context as stressed'). 'Prominent' occurs only in 'prominent positions in government' and the summary-table line above; 'metrical' only inside '(a)symmetrical'; 'accent' never.

3828.dq: Stress is phonemic, e.g., ma'da sun and 'maɣa mountain.
3828.dloc: Appendix 3.7 'Some Phonological Aspects of Kwalean and Manubaran Languages of Rigo', sect. 0.0 and 1.0 p. 916, sect. 2.0 pp. 916-917; Humene (Manugoro) wordlist with primary stress marked, Appendix 3.9 pp. 926-930
3828.prule: Stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive), not positionally predictable. Dutton states it for each Kwalean and Manubaran language of Rigo ('stress seems to be phonemic in each', p. 916) and illustrates it for Kwale with the disyllables ma'da 'sun' (final) vs 'maɣa 'mountain' (initial), p. 917; Humene is said to have a nearly identical phonology. Dutton's own Humene (Manugoro) wordlist (App. 3.9) shows the contrast in Humene itself: most forms carry penultimate stress ('vaʒe, 'maka, 'noka, 'eme, 'ani, o'hoʒe, noʔ'one, o'bude, u'nune, e'mone, ra'fune, e'mere, u'buma, e'vore, go'neva, e'hine...), but several disyllables are stressed on the final syllable (a'bi 'ear' p. 928, o'no 'throat' p. 928, he'ra 'shoulder' p. 929, e'hi 'belly' p. 929), giving the Humene pair 'ehi 'husband' (p. 926, footnote ['ɛhẽ]) vs e'hi 'belly' (p. 929); 'vaoʔai 'old' (p. 926), 'vaene 'jaw' (p. 928) and 'iʔuva 'hair' (p. 930, in oʔ'one 'iʔuva 'chest hair') are stressed on the initial syllable of a 3-4 vowel word. The only stated regularity is that a sequence of like vowels is stressed on its second vowel or broken by a glottal stop (ro'o 'blood', nu'une 'breast', vu'une 'liver'). Language explicitly non-tonal.

3829.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Limi is analysed as a tone language: contrastive tense vs lax phonation plus two tonemes, /rising contour/ vs /falling or level contour/, with the morpheme as tone-bearing unit; in disyllabic morphemes the rising toneme is realised as low-then-mid pitch (pattern (a), n=81/140) against a level pattern (b) (n=40/140). Wilde raises the alternative that (a) vs (b) is second- vs first-syllable stress (the words glossed 'belly' and 'brain'; his proposed re-transcriptions are [cvˈcv] vs [ˈcvcv] (Table 18, p. 63), i.e. second- vs first-syllable stress), finds no length or vowel-quality correlate and only impressionistic, inconsistent intensity differences, and leaves the question open; stress is absent from his list of contrastive prosodic features (p. 65).
3829.srule: Not mentioned in Wilde 2001, secs. 8.6-8.8 (pp. 58-66): the thesis treats only mono- and disyllabic morphemes ('Trisyllabic and quadrisyllabic words are outside the scope of this thesis', p. 59) and leaves even primary stress unresolved ('At this stage I am unable to discuss the issue of stress in further detail', p. 64).

3829.tone: Analysed as tonal: 'The following contrastive prosodic features have been found in Limi: /length/, /nasalisation/, /tense/, /lax/, /rising tone/ and /falling or level tone/' (p. 65); tone-bearing unit = the morpheme, so a rising contour spreads over a disyllable as low-then-mid pitch (pp. 33-34); 'In polymorphemes tone does not spread over morpheme boundaries' (p. 34). On stress the author is explicitly undecided: the disyllabic LM vs level patterns 'possibly [cvˈcv]' vs 'possibly [ˈcvcv]' (Table 18, p. 63) could be re-read as second- vs first-syllable stress tied to tone class, but he finds only 'a minimal difference in intensity' based 'solely on my impression' and concludes 'At this stage I am unable to discuss the issue of stress in further detail' (p. 64). If stress were adopted it would be lexically tied to the toneme (final in rising-tone words, initial in level-tone words), not a positional rule.

3830.prule: No word-stress rule stated. The source marks three tone levels (HIGH, LOW, MID) on every Kihung'an word in its examples and treats the language's focus device as tonal ('tone-focus'), the counterpart of English 'stress-focus'. Nothing in the article says anything about word stress in Kihung'an.

In this paper I will concern myself almost exclusively with Kihung'an, a language in which interesting syntactic features are shared by stress-focus constructions (here manifesting themselves as tone-focus), cleft/pseudo-clefts and relative clauses.

3830.tone: Three tone levels marked (HIGH acute, LOW grave, MID apostrophe) per footnote 1; the language name itself is given as [kíhùŋàn]. The article's only use of 'stress' is for English ('stress-focus', 'stressed under normal intonation', pp. 259-260 and fn. 2); the Kihung'an equivalent is 'tone-focus' throughout section 2 (p. 262 ff.). The source does not discuss stress or accent in Kihung'an. PHOIBLE inventory PH 1114 'Kihungan' (source Takizala 1974) exists for hung1278, but its segment table could not be retrieved (server 406).
